item.title: Getting My Anxious Child to Sleep Is a Bedtime Battle
item.description:
Sleep

Getting My Anxious Child to Sleep Is a Bedtime Battle

For the kid who has bedtime tantrums and mayhem.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Extreme bedtime refusal is a type of tantrum.
  • Bedtime threats of self-harm, suicide, school refusal, and running away are tantrum behaviors.
  • Bedtime tantrums are best treated by strategic inattention.
  • Failing to give attention to tantrums at bedtime helps your child learn to go to sleep without your help.

This is Part 2 of a series. Read Part 1 here.

Sometimes the simpler strategies I mentioned in Part 1 of this post are not enough. Perhaps your kid yells for hours when you try to make them stay in their room, or they keep banging on your door, or they threaten self-harm, run away, refuse to go to school the next day, or even threaten suicide? What then do you do? These behaviors can be overwhelming. You may even wonder if you should take your child to the emergency room for possible psychiatric hospitalization. Doesn’t this mean that something is terribly wrong when they behave this way?

The short answer is both “Yes” and “No.” “Yes” because your child has not developed or has lost their ability to self-regulate and put themselves to sleep, and “No” because they are having a tantrum, which is almost always a situation that can be managed by inattention, even if your child has a mental health condition, neurodivergence, or developmental delay. How you handle these challenging behaviors makes the difference. You might not realize it, but you can learn to do what inpatient and residential programs do and prevent the need for these services.

Step One

Recategorize bedtime yelling, crying, hitting, and threats to run away, self-harm, or refuse to go to school as a tantrum. A tantrum simply means your child is past their capacity for self-control and is bursting loose with words and behaviors to avoid something frustrating. It is an escape attempt to obtain freedom from anticipated frustration (e.g., not being able to get to sleep easily) or gain access to something desired (e.g., more cuddling or co-sleeping). Many children and teens have learned that one way to express extreme distress is to mention suicide, self-harm, or running away. It gets fast results at school and home because adults stop enforcing bedtime rules and instead shift into risk assessment and comfort mode. So, translate any bedtime threat as: “They are just frustrated with bedtime and need to learn self-regulation.”

Step Two

Recognize that any attention you give during a tantrum is toxic for learning self-regulation. That’s right, your efforts to help are only helpful if you step aside and allow your kid to learn to do the thing they are avoiding: to calm themselves down and get to sleep. Nothing you say, whether coaching advice or stern words, is going to help. It just adds mental clutter that distracts from the important task of learning to slow down, calm down, and eventually allow sleep to happen. Your words are, in fact, an irritant. How much did you like your parents talking to you when you were mad? I get goosebumps on the back of my neck when I recall my parents trying to lecture me when they wanted me to do things I disliked. No thanks!

Step Three

Go silent and disappear as soon as the tantrum occurs. You may need to quickly get into a room with a lockable door so you can separate yourself from your kid and keep your reaction hidden. You may need to wear earbuds or noise-canceling headphones. You may need to put away all sharp knives and objects in the car trunk or your bedroom to prevent the opportunity for escalation. The goal is to act like you cannot see, hear, or notice anything your child does while they are having a tantrum. If they run out of the house, let them. The self-imposed discomfort of being outdoors in pajamas with nothing to do will eventually make them choose to return. One of my children chose to “run away” several times, and each time he returned, he slunk back inside, uttered some nasty words which I ignored, and then did the thing he was avoiding. I admit it was amusing for my husband and me to sneak a peek at him through the second-story window, kicking the nearest lamppost, until he hurt his toes and stopped. He cried and cursed but eventually calmed down and came back in, and that was the lesson. He learned he could calm down even when he was furious.

Step Four

Prepare for the tantrum. If you can predict that your child or teen will storm around the house and ruin bedtime and sleep for everyone, you might need to plan for family members to sleep in a quiet area or spend the night at a quiet house while you implement no attention to tantrums. You might want to start this training on the weekend, when you and other caregivers have extra time to catch up on sleep without worrying about waking up for work or school. You might need to sanitize the house or your child’s room by removing objects that can be broken or turned into weapons so they don’t have that option. The idea is to think ahead and prevent opportunities that could throw you off your plan to stay quiet and disappear. I also recommend that partners share the burden by alternating nights so both can avoid getting hopelessly sleep-deprived.

Step Five

Be prepared for the extinction burst. The extinction burst is what happens when the child registers that you have changed your behavior. It is a sign that you are on track and doing the right thing. Most parents confuse this with things getting worse, rather than a predictable sign that the child’s behavior will soon settle. Although they will increase all the words, volume, and behaviors that seem destructive or scary, it only means they are doing one last hurrah to see if they can unseat your new no-attention response. This is when it is most important to stay the course. Your firm, calm response sends a clear message that you're confident they can learn, grow, and develop self-regulation.

Step Six

Most children will make dramatic changes within a two-week period if you consistently stop giving attention to bedtime tantrums. Children who are Level 2 and 3 on the autism spectrum can take longer, but they too learn.

Step Seven

Be prepared to stick to these rules and do not make exceptions, even for illness or vacations. The more you stick to a regular bedtime and consistent rules for lights out and sleeping in your own bed without fuss, the easier it will be for your child to fall asleep and stay asleep.

item.title: How to Run Effective Team Meetings
item.description:
Leadership

How to Run Effective Team Meetings

This quick guide for managers and others can help streamline discussions.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Good meetings begin long before start time, with a distributed agenda and planning.
  • Meetings should begin and end on time, and the organizer should steer the process to increase effectiveness.
  • The leader of a meeting needs to follow up to make sure decisions are executed and all issues are addressed.

Coauthored by Scott J. Allen and Ron Riggio

Running a team meeting is an opportunity for displaying good leadership. You want to communicate effectively, motivate team members, and use the time productively and efficiently. Here are a number of “best practices” and suggestions for running an effective team meeting.

The Agenda

  • Decide the main purpose of the meeting. Is it to make a decision, distribute information, or brainstorm? Make that main purpose known to participants.
  • Keep and distribute the core agenda. Remove completed items, identify items not fully addressed, and add them to the next meeting agenda.
  • Use time efficiently. Consider keeping the meeting to 20- or 45-minute blocks instead of 30- or 60-minute ones. This allows some “buffer” time.

Before the Meeting

  • Send out the agenda 48 hours in advance. Remind participants what they need to bring and what and how they will participate (for example, ask them to provide one-minute updates).
  • Invite only those who need to be at the meeting. Others can get the notes or can decide to attend if they feel the need.
  • Assign a note-taker (for virtual meetings, an AI assistant can do this, but make sure to double-check all notes for accuracy).
  • Arrive 10 minutes early to make sure technology is working and to allow you to greet and connect with attendees.

During the Meeting

  • Remember that you are facilitating the flow of the meeting. Don’t get sucked into the discussion or distracted. Keep things moving and on time.
  • Begin on time, and don’t waste valuable meeting time to “bring latecomers up to speed” (unless it is absolutely necessary).
  • Consider beginning with a quick round of good news and “wins.”
  • Anticipate a timebox for each item (“We have eight minutes for this one”). Make it clear when you have to adjust the timeline if additional minutes are needed on an item.
  • Name a decision when one is made (“OK, we have decided to…”).
  • Assign an “owner” and a timeline on each action item. Say this out loud before moving on to the next item.
  • Watch for silence. Ask directly for input if someone hasn’t spoken on a topic that affects them.
  • At the conclusion, summarize the accomplishments and the significant action items moving forward.
  • End on time. Park leftover items for a follow-up rather than letting the meeting run long.

After the Meeting

  • Send the notes/minutes out immediately.
  • Send reminders to people assigned action items.
  • Periodically, ask one person for honest, unfiltered feedback on the meeting. Entertain their suggestions for improvement.

Common Meeting Pitfalls

  • Is a meeting necessary? Could it have been a one-on-one or an email?
  • Letting unhelpful behaviors slide. If left unaddressed, arriving late, being unprepared, or dominating a discussion can become the norm.
  • Don’t skip the recap/summary, or action items won’t get done.
  • Don't let the meeting run over because of poor facilitation. You are in charge.

item.title: Do Less and Touch Grass
item.description:
Burnout

Do Less and Touch Grass

Unplugging could be the self-care you need.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Many have come to accept feelings of exhaustion as normal and expected.
  • Doing less might sound impossible, but it is a realistic solution to burnout.
  • Doing less is tantamount to self-care; it's a kindness to ourselves we all deserve.
Source: Jorge Urosa / Pexels

Our days are full of countless tasks and endless responsibilities. We have come to accept feelings of exhaustion as normal and expected. We even have adages to describe these experiences: “spreading ourselves thin” and “burning the candle at both ends.”

Though our intentions are good, living life this way often translates to a subpar performance on most of our daily duties. If we take on too much, we simply can’t do it all. What’s the solution?

Do Less

Do less. It might sound impossible, but doing less is actually a realistic solution to burnout. This is not a new idea.

In the 1800s, Vilfredo Pareto, an Italian philosopher and mathematician, developed what would come to be known as the Pareto Principle, or the 80/20 rule. Simply put: Investing in the most important tasks—the top 20 percent—will yield the most significant impact (80 percent of your results). In other words, curating your daily goals to the essentials, meaning those that align with your core values, will allow you to be more successful and feel accomplished. Not only that, doing less actually creates space to live in the moment, connect, and clear your headspace. Instead of “doing” things, you are “being” present. Doing less is tantamount to self-care. It is a kindness to ourselves that we all deserve.

Doing less is not easy. It takes effort. It is an intentional choice every day, sometimes multiple times a day. It requires planning and actually goes against what we think we should be doing. That is because our society is set up to reward tangible accomplishments that we can see.

But what if we reward ourselves for accomplishments that we can feel? Instead of checking off endless tasks to feel productive, try giving yourself a gold star for taking a bath, reading a book for pleasure, calling a friend, going outside, or taking a walk. If we reframe our goals to be inclusive of self-care, we can reclaim our sense of fulfillment beyond those that are rewarded in a capitalistic society. This kind of productivity has real value. These types of daily accomplishments can release dopamine and serotonin levels in your brain and reduce stress, helping you to feel better and more successful.

Touch Grass

Source: kaboompics/Pexels

"Touch grass" has become common slang. I liken it to the much older phrase “stop and smell the roses.” Both may sound silly or cheeky, but they are vital pieces of wisdom.

In today’s handheld device-laden world where we fall down rabbit holes of clickbait, experiencing a temporary high from satisfying our curiosities, it is easy to forget the value of nature. But going outside has proven powerful effects on your brain and your mood. According to one report, just 15 minutes outside can reduce stress by dropping your cortisol levels and increasing the production of “feel-good” chemicals (serotonin and dopamine). Being in nature can also produce a calming effect on the mind.

But touching grass is more than just a literal concept—you don’t actually have to touch grass. The concept of “touching grass” is all about unplugging and being mindful. If nature isn’t your thing, maybe getting creative or playful is. What you do really isn’t important; it’s more about how you do it. The "touch grass" mentality is making the deliberate choice to be present with yourself.

Do Less and Touch Grass

Combining these two practices creates a sense of balance. “Do less and touch grass” gives you permission to be kind to yourself and reward yourself when you are. It is the embodiment of self-care and a reminder that our needs matter.

item.title: 3 Ways Parents Wreck Their Children's Confidence
item.description:
Parenting

3 Ways Parents Wreck Their Children's Confidence

Rescuing, overcorrecting, and pushing can teach kids to doubt themselves.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Rescuing kids too quickly undermines their ability to discover what they can handle.
  • Dismissing children's feelings teaches them to mistrust their own emotional responses.
  • Constantly pushing improvement can leave children feeling scrutinized and evaluated.

As a child and family psychologist, I see how most parents want their children to feel capable, secure, and ready for life. Yet, some of the things we do out of love send an unintended message. That message is: "You can't handle this" or "You're wrong to feel that way." Yet another problematic message is: "You are only good enough when you succeed." Having spent thousands of hours listening to struggling adult children and their parents, I hear how painful these messages are and the long-term negative impacts they cause.

A Long History of Emotional Pain

In my work with children, teens, and adults, I have seen how deeply those messages can land and burrow into a child's belief system. Adult children sometimes describe parents who cared intensely ("Yeah, I know they love me, but they don't get who I really am"). Specifically, many adult children look back on their childhoods and, while describing parents who cared intensely, they say there was little room for mistakes, uncomfortable feelings, or independent decisions.

I'm not saying these accounts explain every struggle, so please don't think, "Here goes Dr. Jeff blaming parents for everything," because that is not the case. Temperament, peers, and life experiences matter too. But our everyday response as parents is a huge place to make a difference. Below are three patterns to watch for, and what to do instead.

1. You Rescue Them Before They Discover What They Can Handle

While researching my recent book, The Rescue Trap: How Well-Meaning Parents Keep Their Adult Children Stuck, I reflected a lot on parents who quickly step in, smooth things over, and reflexively solve their kids' problems. It may have started with a forgotten assignment, struggles with friendship, or even feeling nervous about speaking to someone. Yes, sometimes parent intervention is necessary. But when rescue becomes the default, children lose opportunities to experience something essential: "This was hard, and I handled it." Or, let's not forget that "This did not work out the way I would have liked, but I will learn from it" provides lots of value too.

What I am saying is that repeated rescuing can make your confidence in them harder to see than your concern. As I say to a lot of parents I coach, there is a difference between carrying your kid (at any age) and caring for them. So, how about offering support without immediately taking over? You could say something like, "That sounds uncomfortable. What do you think your first step could be?" For a younger child, maybe you could practice saying those words together. Whereas for a teen, you could guide them in weighing their options. The goal here is to provide enough support for them to take the next step themselves while also letting them learn through trial and error.

2. You Turn Their Feelings Into Something They Need to Defend

Saying, "You're being too sensitive" or "You have nothing to worry about," or the biggest offender, "You shouldn't feel that way," may be a parent's attempt to provide reassurance. But children, teens, and adult children often hear, "My reactions aren't acceptable, and I cannot trust myself." Keep in mind that confidence includes learning to understand your feelings without letting them rule you. That becomes challenging when every uncomfortable emotion leads to a debate or an argument.

I have written a good deal about how overthinking is laden with cycles of second-guessing, where it is harder for kids to move forward. A parent can offer a place to pause and find a next workable step. For example, the parent could say, "I could see why that was really upsetting. Let's look at what happened and if there are some other ways to understand it and learn from it." This means you can validate painful emotions like disappointment without agreeing that the world is against your child. Similarly, you can empathize with their anxiety without treating every new situation as dangerous.

3. You Make Improvement the Loudest Message of the Relationship

It is really tough for many parents when they notice missed test questions, slipping grades, a messy room, or a response that isn't fully honest. Each correction you encourage seems reasonable as you trumpet the message, "All I want to see is that you try your best." By the way, I will confess that I have not always tried my best. Have you always tried your best? Let's not dismiss the value of strong effort, but what if your child feels constantly scrutinized and evaluated?

When praise is quickly followed by "but," your child's brain stores the accomplishment as a reminder of what's still "wrong." Some children may push themselves harder and chase perfection, while others stop studying and shut down. How about saying more things like: "I like how you stayed with that even when you were frustrated" or "I know you are disappointed, but I appreciate how you took responsibility."

The Takeaway

Children of all ages need guidance and boundaries to help them make solid choices. They also need room to struggle, grapple with feelings, and learn without feeling like their worth is being put on trial. The next time you feel compelled to step in, slow down, pause, and ask: "Will what I do help my child trust their own ability, or will it make them more likely to rely on my help?"

item.title: When the Quiet One in the Relationship Starts to Bite Back
item.description:
Relationships

When the Quiet One in the Relationship Starts to Bite Back

What happens when the one who withdraws gets tired of being the problem.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • The attack-attack pattern begins when the withdrawer gets tired of taking the blame.
  • Both partners feel hurt and defensive, turning against each other instead of reaching out.
  • Understanding each partner’s fears helps shift from criticism to emotional honesty.
  • Emotionally Focused Therapy helps couples replace defensiveness with vulnerability and mutual comfort.

In my work as a couples therapist, I often see a distinct pattern in couples who have been together for a while. After years of engaging in a pursue/withdraw pattern (aka the anxious/avoidant attachment dance), sometimes the withdrawer starts to get sick and tired of feeling steamrolled or like they are always the problem. They start to bite back. This is how the attack-attack pattern happens in relationships.

The attack-attack pattern features a pursuer (someone who tends to present as angry in conflict) and a defensive partner who counterattacks. While the pursuer is often the one to confront with demands or criticisms, the defensive partner responds with the same put-downs. It’s important to note that each is motivated by slightly different feelings and aims. Let’s look at an example (this is an amalgamation of many couples I've seen in therapy rather than an actual couple).

Sue is a pursuer. She often worries about abandonment in their relationship and is preoccupied with questions of, “Do I matter to my partner? Does he really want to be with me? Does he care about me?”

These fears are triggered in her relationship with John when he stays late at work. She is consumed with fears of being unloved and less important to John than his work. When she’s triggered, Sue gets loud, puts down John, and demands that he stop working so late, or else.

John is a former withdrawer turned defensive attacker. He has a demanding job, but he feels a sense of competence from conquering his challenges at work. What he hears when Sue protests his work hours is, “You aren’t good enough. You can’t meet my needs. You are failing, and you just might lose me because of it.”

What John used to do when he heard these messages was withdraw. He would shut down and hide, and sometimes what this would look like was him retreating into work, where he felt good about himself and that he was not failing. But John has become sick and tired of always feeling like the problem, so he’s started to bite back. Instead of turning away and hiding, John now turns to Sue and says, “You know what, you aren’t such an angel yourself. What about how you came home an hour late after hanging out with your girlfriends last night? I’m not the only one who comes home late!”

Such patterns are often confusing to both partners. John is confused by his new way of responding, and his self-image is rocked. While he used to see himself as a gentle man who valued harmony and would never criticize his wife, he is confused by the new feelings of frustration that have replaced his shame. Sue is shocked—she’s never seen her husband this angry before. The status quo of the relationship has shifted.

When I see this pattern in relationships, it’s a clear sign that partners need to turn toward each other in more vulnerable and authentic ways. What is happening in the attack-attack pattern is that both are turning against each other, while one used to turn away.

An emotionally focused (EFT) therapist will help you learn to share your feelings and needs in a more authentic and vulnerable way so you can break out of patterns of criticism and defensiveness. Sue will learn how to share her needs to feel close and loved, in a way that motivates John will learn to meet them rather than feeling he has to defend himself. John will learn to speak from his own experience about not feeling good enough so that Sue can comfort him rather than feel triggered by his responses. And that’s how attack/attack turns into mutual turning toward.

item.title: You Can Care Deeply Without Carrying It All
item.description:
Codependency

You Can Care Deeply Without Carrying It All

It's possible to care without making someone else's experience yours to manage.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Being responsive to someone’s feelings is not the same as being responsible for them.
  • Noticing provides an opportunity to pause, separate what belongs to someone else, and choose how to respond.
  • The UNPLUG practice helps people stay connected and compassionate without carrying what isn’t theirs.

Everyone around us is navigating something. You can probably think of a time when a colleague walked into work frustrated, and you suddenly felt tense; when your child came home from school in a terrible, no-good, rotten mood; or when your partner was carrying worries that started to weigh on you, too.

On a recent podcast episode, I answered a question I think many of us have wondered: Am I allowed to be happy when someone I care about isn't? That someone could be your child, partner, parent, friend, colleague, or team.

My answer is yes, you are, but I think part of this requires us to understand the difference between caring about someone's experience and carrying it for them.

When Did You Become the Happiness Coordinator?

A person who has taken on the role of happiness coordinator may come to believe it's their job to make sure everyone around them is okay, or even happy. If someone is upset, disappointed, or frustrated, they want to do something about it right away. It is only when everyone is content and okay that they feel they can finally exhale. A few often overlapping patterns can lead us into believing this is our responsibility:

  • Early learning: If you monitored a parent’s mood or were the one who kept the peace at home, you may have picked up the idea that if someone is unhappy, it is your job to fix it.
  • Being highly attuned: Noticing slight changes in someone’s tone, the look on their face, or a shift in their mood can be a strength. This emotional attunement can also be exhausting when our first instinct is that something is wrong and we feel like we need to do something about it.
  • We measure ourselves by how others feel: We might believe that we are a good parent, partner, or leader only if everyone around us is happy.
  • Confusing empathy and support with responsibility: In close relationships especially, “I can be with you while you feel this” can start to blur into “You’re hurting, therefore I need to feel bad too and figure out how to make you feel better.”
  • It gives a sense of control: If someone is upset and we believe we need to fix it, we’ve given ourselves a job to do. If we solve or remove the problem for them and they feel better, we feel a sense of relief, and our brain learns that managing other people’s feelings makes our own anxiety go away.

What Happens When We "Catch" an Emotion?

Sometimes, we may not even notice ourselves picking up on the emotions of those around us right away. Emotional contagion is the tendency to automatically mimic another person's emotions and behaviours (Hatfield et al., 1994). It can happen between individuals and within groups, often outside our awareness.

Let's say your shoulders tense the moment your frustrated colleague walks in, or your mood shifts when your child comes through the door upset, despite your relatively smooth afternoon. Your nervous system is doing what nervous systems do. This initial response may not be a choice, yet what happens next can be.

Once you notice that you've picked up someone else's emotional state, my gentle invitation is to get curious about where their feeling ends and yours begins. We can notice their experience without taking it on ourselves, fixing it immediately, or staying emotionally caught up in it with them.

Holding Space Without Carrying It

Holding space means being there with someone while they feel what they're feeling. We can acknowledge what they're going through without feeling like we have to take ownership of it.

The reality is that carrying someone else's emotional experience isn't a deeper form of caring. It is actually what can leave us feeling emotionally stretched and make caring harder to sustain over time. Just as we might need a way to mentally leave a difficult workday at the door before coming home, we also need ways to set down an emotion that isn't ours to carry.

The UNPLUG Practice

To create a little space between their experience and your emotional state, my gentle invitation is for you to try the UNPLUG practice. Of course, we still care deeply, but we don't carry their experience in a way that ruins our mood or turns it into something that is our responsibility to fix.

  • U: Understand what's happening: Notice when someone else's emotions have become your own. Try checking in with yourself: Was I feeling this way before they walked into the room?
  • N: Name what's yours: Separate their experience from your response. For example, "My child is disappointed. I'm feeling anxious about their disappointment."
  • P: Pause your physiological response: Before responding, settle your own nervous system. Regulate your own body before trying to help them regulate theirs. Feel your feet on the floor, relax your jaw, and take a few slow breaths with a longer exhale.
  • L: Let them have their feelings: When someone we care about is struggling, it is natural for us to want to take away the frustration, disappointment, hurt, or discomfort as quickly as we can. What can be helpful is to resist the urge to immediately fix, jump in, or rescue, and get curious about what they need instead. You might try: "I can see you're really disappointed. Do you want me to listen, help you think it through, or give you some space?"
  • U: Understand your responsibility: Ask yourself what is actually required of you. Are they in danger? Do they need practical help? Can they navigate this themselves? Often, our presence, a listening ear, and the space to work through it themselves can be enough.
  • G: Give yourself permission to return to your life: You don't have to stay distressed to prove that you care. If they're working through something hard, you can still go back to your book, enjoy your dinner, take a walk, or laugh with a friend. You can still care about what they are going through and be there if they need you, without making their emotional state the condition for your well-being.

If the whole practice feels like a lot, start with the first two. I think if we can just "UN" by understanding what's going on and naming what's ours, it can make a difference in how we respond and show up for them in the moment.

Final Thoughts

Allowing ourselves to care without carrying it all means being present, compassionate, and responsive without believing it's our job to always fix how someone else feels. The emotions and experiences of the people we care about can be real and matter without automatically becoming ours to hold in every moment.

item.title: The Need for More Awareness During ADHD Awareness Month
item.description:
ADHD

The Need for More Awareness During ADHD Awareness Month

A lack of understanding and support for people with ADHD means we all miss out.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disability that affects regions of the brain related to executive functions.
  • A lack of understanding and adequate support from society leads to higher rates of adverse outcomes.
  • Because ADHDers are rarely set up to succeed, everyone misses out on their strengths.

A fifth grader sits with her parents across from her teacher during conferences. The teacher shares how well she is doing in school but points out the significant variations in her state test scores over the course of elementary school. “Now you need to work on getting more consistent scores on your state tests.” The teacher is unaware that these score patterns are common for people with ADHD, and that the student will never be able to meet this goal.

A social worker with ADHD is behind on paperwork again. His supervisor calls him into her office and tells him that if he can’t meet paperwork expectations, he should ask himself if social work is the right profession for him.

A teen is playing a board game with friends. “Hand me the um…what are they called? The white cube things.” Their friend looks at them with derision. “You mean the dice?” and then hands them over while everyone teases them for forgetting basic vocabulary, not realizing that this is part of their ADHD.

A woman in her late 40s who was just diagnosed with ADHD is asked at work what accommodations she needs at her new job. She tells them she is new to this and doesn’t know, so no accommodations are given. Within a few months, she is at risk of being fired due to struggles with organization and time management.

A man’s insurance changes, and the new policy will not cover his ADHD medication. He is told he has to switch to a cheaper option. The new medication is less effective, and he quickly starts having trouble managing his workplace duties. He goes back to his doctor, who helps him submit a request to go back on the previous medication, but the insurance company sends back a denial. He loses his job a few months later.

A kindergartner sits at circle time during the first week of school. He is struggling to be still and keep his hands to himself. The teacher speaks harshly to him several times and then separates him from everyone else. He feels like his teacher and classmates are laughing at him. In the years to come, when he thinks about his struggles in school that end with him dropping out at 16, he will remember this as the moment he knew he would hate school.

A woman rattles off the week’s schedule to her husband Sunday night, including that she needs him to get the kids ready on Thursday so that they can leave for an event right when she gets home. Thursday night comes around, and she finds her husband watching a cartoon with the kids and no one is ready to go. “I told you I needed the kids to be ready tonight! Why do I have to do everything?” Her husband looks confused and does not remember the conversation from four days before.

Source: Yan Krukau / Pexels

The Realities of ADHD

When people think of ADHD, they often assume that this means a person cannot sit still or pay attention. The reality is much more complicated. ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disability that affects a number of regions in the brain. Research has revealed differences in brain structures and operations that directly affect executive functions, including:

  • Differences in the structure and size of regions such as the cerebellum, corpus callosum, caudate nucleus, overall right hemisphere, and frontal regions
  • Less blood flow in the prefrontal cortex
  • A two- to three-year delay in brain maturation in certain regions, especially in the frontal lobes, putting the person’s executive functions about two to three years behind their same-age peers
  • Below-normal transmission of dopamine and norepinephrine

All of these factors can impact the person’s executive functioning abilities and skills.

What Are Executive Functions?

While there is no agreed-upon definition of executive functions, a list created by Peg Dawson and Richard Guare in their Smart, but Scattered series is a helpful place to start. This list includes 10 executive functions: response inhibition, working memory, emotional control, sustained attention, task initiation, planning/prioritization, organization, time management, goal-directed persistence, flexibility, metacognition, and stress tolerance. For people with ADHD, except for flexibility and stress tolerance, which tend to be easier for them, performing many of these executive functions can be very difficult.

Look back at the scenarios above. These are based on the real struggles of real people with ADHD. As you review them, you can see how struggles with executive functions can present in a variety of ways and have significant impacts on the individual.

Society’s Lack of Understanding and Support Can Increase the Severity of the Disability

Lack of understanding from society adds to the difficulties that come along with ADHD. Because of this lack, this community is often set up to fail.

This is backed up by the research, as we see that people with ADHD experience:

  • Higher rates of co-occurring mental health diagnoses
  • Higher rates of unemployment and job loss
  • Increased likelihood of legal issues
  • Decreased likelihood of engaging in preventive healthcare
  • Higher rates of obesity
  • Higher divorce rates
  • Elevated high school and college dropout rates
  • Higher injury rates
  • Higher incidence of traffic accidents
  • Higher suicidality

Due to these potential experiences, research has shown that untreated ADHD can reduce life expectancy by as much as 13 years.

Society’s Lack of Understanding and Support Means We All Miss Out

Because of the lack of understanding from society as a whole, we also miss out on the strengths that come from this neurodivergent group. For the same reasons that ADHDers struggle with a number of executive functions, they also excel in many areas. People with ADHD are more likely to be out-of-the-box thinkers and often seek novelty. This makes them more likely to be entrepreneurs and to find new and innovative solutions to problems. They are often funny and can energize group dynamics. They tend to be more flexible and to perform better in stressful situations. These strengths are things that we miss out on when we fail to set ADHDers up for success. So, for ADHD Awareness Month, take some time to learn more about this dynamic group and how we as a society can grow our awareness and ensure that this community is adequately accommodated. If we do, we will all benefit.

item.title: How to Create Trust When Communicating in an AI World
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

How to Create Trust When Communicating in an AI World

Learn to protect yourself and your company.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Digital notarization will become crucial as AI use expands in business communication.
  • Shared passwords for validation will secure synchronous communication in the AI era.
  • Institutional trust may become a key competitive differentiator in an AI-driven market.

In Ancient Rome, notaries were used to provide trust. Today, as AI use expands in business, digital notarization will be increasingly important.

Communication Methods in Ancient Rome

Ancient Romans communicated in synchronous and asynchronous channels. Synchronous channels involved face-to-face interaction. Asynchronous communication involved writing on parchment, papyrus, or stone. The document was then delivered to an individual.

Because most people could not read, a trusted third party was needed to verify the authenticity of critical asynchronous communications. History’s first recognized notary was Marcus Tullius Tiro (74-4BC), a Roman slave freed by Cicero.

Notaries were critical to preventing fraud and maintaining citizen confidence. This structured approach to validating asynchronous communication helped the Roman Empire expand international trade.

In 2000, we still had synchronous and asynchronous communication channels. Synchronous communication involved face-to-face, voice over telephone, or images over the internet. As in ancient Roman times, people tended to believe what they could see, hear, and directly verify.

Asynchronous communication moved to paper and to digital formats. Important legal communications continued to be officially notarized by an impartial notary to verify validity.

Communications in Today’s AI Business Environment

We are now in the beginning stages of a serious disruption to traditional communication. Synchronous communication still can be face-to-face, over telephone, or online. But employees will have rising levels of reservations about the validity of such communications. For example: “I just had an online meeting with my boss. She instructed me to wire corporate funds to the XYZ Corporation. Was I really speaking with my boss? Maybe it was a bot pretending to be my boss."

How can meaningful business be conducted when you no longer can trust what you see or hear?

Passwords for Synchronous Communication

In this new AI world, employees will create passwords between team members to validate synchronous communication via phone or internet. For example: “Boss, you are instructing me to wire funds to XYZ Corporation. Of course, I will do as instructed. Before I execute, tell me the name of your college roommate.”

These shared passwords should be verbally communicated and not put online like passwords we use on the internet. AI today can break into online documentation.

Three Critical Asynchronous Communication Spheres

Victor Cho is CEO and founder of Emovid, a human-verified asynchronous communication platform. He states that there are three asynchronous areas where 21st-century notarization will be as critical as notaries were for Ancient Rome: sensitive communications, security flow, and customer trust.

  • Sensitive corporate communications. It is vital to stakeholders that critical written and visual messages be authenticated to remove concerns about AI sabotage. For example, over the weekend, all employees receive an email from the company president announcing a 20 percent reduction of the workforce starting Monday. Was that message really from the President?
  • Security flows. This might include orders for wire transfers or emails from customers asking for shipments to unusual addresses.
  • Customer trust. When a customer is talking with a company agent, how important is it that the agent is a verified human? If making a restaurant reservation, it might not matter. If your teenager has attempted suicide, you want to be talking to a human when you dial 911.

“We will reach this point where we no longer will know if we are talking with a real person or a bot," Cho says. "But knowing that the person is indeed human will be an important factor in stakeholder trust.”

Institutional Trust as a Competitive Edge

In an earlier Psychology Today post, we argued that as AI becomes more widely used in business, it will be increasingly difficult for companies to compete in the marketplace based on analytical superiority or unique technology. Perceived institutional trust will become the critical differentiator for customer retention. (Stybel Peabody, 2025).

Conclusion

The Roman Empire found notaries an important tool for citizen trust. It facilitated international commerce. As AI utilization expands in business, the need for notaries will increase. The form of notarization will increasingly be digital.

Those companies wishing to be on the leading edge of perceived stakeholder trust will also want to be in the vanguard of digital notarization. Companies should begin thinking about having verbal secret passwords between team members to confirm the validity of online and phone interactions. These verbal passwords should not be shared online.

item.title: Effective Flirting Looks Different for Men and Women
item.description:
Flirting

Effective Flirting Looks Different for Men and Women

Effective flirting strategies differ by sex and context.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Men and women who seek to attract potential partners often initiate contact using some flirtation strategy.
  • The effectiveness of different flirting strategies will depend on who's flirting, and for what purpose.
  • Effective strategies are quite consistent across cultures and individual personalities.
Source: Sunriseforever/Pixabay

Men and women who seek to attract potential partners for either short-term hookups or long-term romantic relationships often initiate contact using some flirtation strategy, which may involve verbal (opening lines, humor) or nonverbal (dress, dance moves, smile, gift-giving) behavior.

Human flirtation, we may note, is unique within the animal kingdom, in which males seek to attract a potential mate’s attention by honestly representing their quality, allowing females to choose the best males by selecting those that produce the highest-intensity signals. Human flirting behavior, however, is characterized by subtlety, ambiguity, and covertness. Why would that be?

University of Pennsylvania psychologists Andrew Gersick and Robert Kurzban (2014) proposed that the explanation is rooted in the potential social costs of human flirting to all involved: judgment, hostility, rejection, humiliation, reputational damage, etc. In this view, flirters who are flexible and socially attuned, adjusting to social context and minimizing risk, are viewed by the receivers favorably, signaling that they possess broader behavioral flexibility and social intelligence, both of which are highly adaptive, and hence valued in potential human partners.

So, human flirtation is nuanced and tactical. The question arises as to the nature and effectiveness of different flirtation tactics: Do different approaches work for men vs. women, or in short- vs. long-term quests? One way to understand and evaluate flirting behavior is via the Sexual Strategies Theory (SST) perspective, which argues that different mate acquisition tactics will prove most efficient depending on sex and the mating context (short- or long-term). Thus, for example, cues to sexual availability should prove more effective when used by women in a short-term mating context. Conversely, acts of generosity that denote commitment and investment will prove more effective when used by men in a long-term mating context.

A series of four studies by U.S. researchers T. Joel Wade and Jennifer Slemp (2015) explored how men and women flirt and the effectiveness of different approaches. Study 1 (n = 40) and Study 2 (n = 60) looked at how men and women, respectively, indicate romantic interest to a partner. Study 3 (n = 110) sought to determine which female flirtatious acts are perceived as most effective by men. Study 4 (n = 222) sought to determine which male flirtatious acts are perceived as most effective by women. The results of Studies 1 and 2 showed that flirtations for long- and short-term relationships did not differ. The list of flirtatious acts for males was longer than that generated for females (26 vs. 14). Study 3 found that the items: “She kisses you on the cheek,” “She rubs against you,” “She moves closer to you,” “She touches you, in general,” and “She touches your arm” were rated as most effective. While results for Study 4 revealed that the items: “He holds hands with you,” “He spends time with you,” “He asks you out,” “He makes you laugh,” “He kisses you,” “He acts interested in you,” and “He has dinner with you” were rated as most effective.

In sum, the authors note that, as SST would predict, “Flirtations from women that suggest sexual access and flirtations from men that suggest exclusivity, commitment, and caring were perceived as the most effective flirtatious acts.”

More recently (2022), Norwegian researcher Leif Edward Ottesen Kennair and colleagues used Norwegian and U.S. convenience samples (N = 415 and 577, respectively) of heterosexual participants who answered survey questions about 40 different flirtation tactics, as well as their socio-sexuality, mate value, extraversion, religiosity, and demographics. Each participant responded to one of four flirtation scenarios, presented randomly:

  1. A woman flirting for short-term sex with a man
  2. A woman flirting for a long-term relationship with a man
  3. A man flirting for short-term sex with a woman
  4. A man flirting for a long-term relationship with a woman

Results showed that sexual availability cues (e.g., physical contact, display of body, and sexy dress) were rated more effective than friendly contact (such as hugs or kissing on the cheek) or humor when used by women in short-term mating contexts. Cues for generosity and commitment, as well as humor and taking part in intimate conversations, were judged most effective when used by men in long-term mating contexts. Laughing or giggling at someone's jokes was an effective flirtation tactic for both sexes.

Six tactics overlapped on the top 10 lists for women and men in the short-term context. However, the most effective tactics for women were exclusively sexual or physical, while men were judged more effective if they also smiled, showed interest in conversations, gave compliments, and made the woman laugh. For long-term mating, the top 10 male and female tactics were almost identical (overlap: 9 of 10).

Overall, individual differences (such as extraversion, mate value, and religiosity) did not meaningfully predict flirting effectiveness. And while some cultural differences were found (for example, the U.S. sample rated bodily displays, initial contact, and generosity as more effective flirting techniques), they were overshadowed by the robust differences based on sex and mating context, hinting at the evolved biological dispositions underneath the widespread behavioral patterns.

item.title: The Rise of the Term 'Situationship'
item.description:
Mating

The Rise of the Term 'Situationship'

A word that perfectly captures many modern relationships enters the mainstream.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • The "situationship" label captures relationship ambiguity, gaining traction since its 2008 debut.
  • The word "situationship" originated in England in 2008 and has seen a significant rise in usage since 2023.
  • Urban Dictionary has featured other "-ship" terms, but none have been as widely accepted as "situationship."
Situationships can be difficult to navigate
Source: Grok / xAi

Consider, for a moment, the wide variety of terms that we use to talk about attraction and interpersonal connection. English has many such words, and the stock of vocabulary we use to describe them continues to expand.

Terms Denoting Intimacy

In some cases, these emotional connections are mostly or completely one-sided, and we use terms like crush or infatuation to describe them.

In other cases, the attraction may be mutual but short-lived. When it involves two young people, for example, we may say that this is "just a case of puppy love."

Terms like fling or dalliance also imply short-term pairings, albeit of a more intimate nature, while entanglements can be complicated romances that continue over a longer period of time.

The umbrella term relationship has existed in English since at least 1724, although it initially referred to any kind of association. Its emergence as a way to describe an emotional or romantic connection is surprisingly recent: Its earliest attestation by the Oxford English Dictionary dates to 1944.

As a term, “relationship” is unsatisfying because it’s too broad: Romantic partners are in a relationship, but so are ex-partners, as well as family members, friends, and colleagues. We often have to qualify the term, perhaps by stating that we have a “close” or a “distant” relationship with someone. In addition, the variety of intimate relationships can be quite diverse, so a generic label isn’t very satisfying or even particularly useful.

Facebook famously recognized this problem and attempted to address it: The company added It’s complicated to its lineup of relationship status options in early 2006. The ambiguity of the term made it surprisingly useful, and the phrase entered the vernacular as a shorthand for characterizing many types of on-again/off-again liaisons.

Some relationship terms refer unambiguously to physical intimacy. The phrase friends with benefits (FWB) has been around since the late 1990s, and comedian Bill Bellamy popularized booty call during the same decade. Hooking up, on the other hand, is notoriously problematic, since it can be used to describe a wide variety of interactions, ranging from just spending time with someone to explicit sexual activity.

The Rise of "Situationship"

As it happens, a new relationship term is having its moment.

According to the Nexis Uni database, it first appeared in print in the Western Daily Press, a regional paper in southwest England, in March 2008. During an interview, the Welsh TV presenter Josie d’Arby was asked about her favorite word. She replied, “I should say the word I invented myself— ‘situationship'—it’s like a relationship but less serious” ("In the Hot Seat", 2008).

Five years later, in November 2013, the term cropped up again in the pages of Marie Claire magazine. A 31-year-old woman named Erica related that “For the past five years, I’ve been with this same guy, but he won’t commit—I call it a ‘situationship,’ not even a ‘relationship’” ("Most Awkward", 2013). It’s interesting to note that, in both early cases, the speakers themselves claimed to have coined the term—and they may well have done so independently.

In early 2014, it popped up again in the British version of the TV game show "Deal or No Deal." A transcript of the episode captured a contestant saying “Ah! I’m in a ‘situationship.’ That is one of these modern words!” (Edmonds, 2014).

Some early references to the term hyphenate it (situation-ship), or place it between quotation marks, or provide a brief gloss about its meaning. A 2016 article in Medium, for example, employed all these devices (Olojo, 2016). Linguistic chaperones such as these often accompany new terms as they make their debuts.

But after only sporadic and limited usage during the 2010s, situationship began to break out. This can be quantified by its uptake in high-circulation newspapers and magazines.

The New York Times, for example, first employed it in a mid-2016 article about an episode of "Empire," Fox’s musical drama series. The editors chose to bracket the term in quotation marks and also provided a definition (“not an official relationship but maybe more than friends with benefits” (Best, 2016). But over the next six years, the paper employed the term only seven times. In 2023, however, situationship appeared in a dozen articles, and by 2025 The Times was employing it, on average, twice a month.

A similar pattern of usage appears in The Washington Post. Its reporters first employed the term in early 2018: “Melissa was fine with casual at first, but eventually she wanted to label their ‘situationship’” (Birch, 2018). After that, it appeared only sporadically, but then usage accelerated in 2023 and 2024.

The Atlantic also began to use the word with some frequency, starting in 2025. And if we examine articles published on the Psychology Today website, we see that usage of the term tripled between 2024 and 2025. Situationship was even one of four finalists in Oxford University Press’s 2023 Word of the Year competition—although it was beaten out by rizz (a shortened form of charisma).

Situationship is clearly derived from “relationship,” and -ship is a very flexible suffix, adept at attaching itself to a variety of nouns (citizenship, companionship, craftsmanship). It’s not surprising, then, to see it spinning off additional interpersonal terms. But very few of these—and possibly none—will gain enough traction to enter the language as full-time, dues-paying members.

As one example, Urban Dictionary recorded crush-ship as far back as 2010, and delusionship appeared in a USA Today story in mid-2023. Crushship, however, hasn’t yet appeared in The Times, The Post, or Psychology Today, and delusionship has cropped up in The Post just once, in 2023. Whatever their merits, these other terms lack the quintessence of ambiguity that makes situationship so useful.

item.title: The Complex Vicious Cycle of Loneliness
item.description:
Loneliness

The Complex Vicious Cycle of Loneliness

Recent research shows how easy it is to get stuck in a rut.

Posted October 1, 2026

Loneliness has gotten an increasing amount of research attention as of late, with the role of social connection being studied more and more in terms of its impact on both physical and mental health. Loneliness has been declared an epidemic in certain countries, and the public health focus on it — including attention given by former U.S. Surgeon General Dr. Vivek Murthy — has been growing over recent years.

Loneliness raises your risk not only of certain mental health conditions like depression and anxiety, but it is also associated with poorer physical health — from a higher risk of cardiovascular disease to increased inflammation and decreased immune function. Being lonely needs to be defined carefully, however. Whenever I give talks on the health benefits of social support, there is someone who at first assumes that I am prizing the idea of having a lot of friends over having only a few, or suggesting constant socializing rather than savoring time alone. Neither of those concepts speaks to true loneliness. The most popular person at the party who counts dozens of people as friends might be lonelier than the person who has only three people they ever confide in, for instance. The question that determines loneliness is whether you are satisfied and nourished by the connections that you do have, no matter how plentiful they are. Are they giving you what you need?

Compounding the problem of loneliness is the fact that it can easily slide into a vicious cycle. The more lonely you are, the more distressed you may feel — making it harder to put yourself into the types of situations that can grow connection, create relationships, and instill belonging. For a lot of depressed or anxious people, this is the rut that can make them feel more and more helpless. They don't feel energized or optimistic enough to attend the new-student outing or the neighborhood block party, for example, in part because they are already lonely — which robs them further of the opportunity to create new friendships. And the cycle spins on.

Now, recent research further illuminates that that cycle may be even more complicated, and may involve their perception in the moments of interaction themselves. In a study that appeared in the February 2026 edition of Communications Psychology, loneliness appeared to affect people's actual assessment of whether they were being rejected. 157 adults spanning ages 46 to 74 were studied over the course of 20 days. They received text messages at five randomized times per day that prompted them to take a survey assessing their loneliness, levels of self-disclosure and their perceived social rejection, among other characteristics. The connection was clear: being more lonely as a general trait meant people were more likely to assess any given reaction as having included rejection, which in turn would make them at greater risk for feeling lonely later. The lonelier you were, the more you were assessing situations as rejecting, and the less you were trying to go deeper within them. Lonely people were also less likely to self-disclose in those situations, making it even more unlikely that they would be able to connect over time.

These findings and others emphasize that loneliness isn't likely one specific, stable state — it's a process that keeps playing out in real time, and affects the environment and thoughts that individuals are subjected to on a daily basis. But if support can be sought out early, and people can take a step out of their comfort zone and recognize, perhaps, that their perceptions of whether they are being rejected may be somewhat distorted, then they may be able to stop the slippery slope in the process — and enjoy better health because of it.

item.title: Why Kids Lie, Steal, and Curse, and What Parents Can Do
item.description:
Parenting

Why Kids Lie, Steal, and Curse, and What Parents Can Do

Learn what’s driving children's “bad” behaviors so you can respond effectively.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • When kids lie, steal, or curse, they may be trying to express feelings they can’t put into words.
  • Children often attempt to make others feel how they feel as a way of expressing themselves.
  • Under these so-called "bad" behaviors lie intense feelings that kids are struggling to manage.

There’s a reason kids behave badly, and it’s not to make their parents crazy. Why they behave badly usually isn’t clear to parents or their kids, but just know that their bad behavior makes sense once we understand what’s driving the behavior. At the root of a kid’s acting out are always emotions as well as a message or desire they’re trying to communicate. That message or the emotions often get lost because the bad behavior gets all the attention. But if only the behavior gets our attention—and not the child’s feelings, which create the acting-out behaviors—then the child will continue to behave badly. Nothing will change, and the two of you will get stuck in a downward spiral of bad behavior, hurt feelings, and negative narratives that could develop into serious self-esteem issues for your child.

Here’s what’s really going on with three specific, common behaviors, what you can do to stop them, and how you can help your child develop better ways of acting and communicating.

Lying

Why it happens. Kids under five are often not lying per se because, developmentally, they don’t have a firm grip on what is real versus imagined. Instead, they’re often expressing their fantasy of what they wish were true.

Older kids, however, will often lie because they feel shame. It’s not that they are dishonest at their core; they are ashamed of the truth, whether it’s something they did or said.

How to handle it. Speak to the shame without further shaming. You might say, “I know how the bowl got broken, because I heard you bouncing the basketball. I’m sad the bowl broke, but I don’t think you’re a bad kid. I know you didn’t mean to break anything, and I know you feel bad. I think the ball got out of control, and from now on, it stays outside. It’s OK to feel bad about what happened, but just know that doesn’t change my mind about you: I still think you’re a great kid, even when you make mistakes.”

Stealing

Why it happens. Frequently, kids steal because they feel a loss or want others to feel a loss. (Note: Kids under five may simply and unemotionally covet the object they’re stealing.) In older kids, however, there’s an emotional component: They are either expressing their emotions or trying to elicit emotions in others, especially the person who loses the stolen object.

How to handle it. First, ask yourself if your child might be experiencing a loss of some kind. The loss can be general (i.e., the family struggles financially) or specific (i.e., the loss of a friend). Rather than focus on the stealing, focus on the child’s loss, and name it. You might say, “When you took my mom’s photo from my desk and hid it, it made me miss her even more, and now I see how much you’re missing your friend who moved away.”

A note about why kids can be poor thieves: Once, a 7-year-old client was stealing candy from his older brother and hiding the wrappers under his pillow. While he denied the thefts, his parents quickly discovered the wrappers. This was a bright kid, so why was he such a bad thief—a “good” thief gets rid of the evidence, right? Why hide the wrappers in a place that so clearly implicated him?

I believe there was a part of this child that wanted to be caught, that wanted his family to know how much he wanted something that his older brother had. It was the child’s way of communicating his needs. He wasn’t trying to say, “Look, I’m a dishonest thief!” He was trying to say, “Look, my brother has things I want and need. I would like them, too!” In this specific case, the older brother had just been diagnosed with a significant medical issue and was naturally receiving a lot of his parents’ attention, and the younger child felt quite forgotten. He wasn’t a thief; he was only sad and worried.

Cursing

Why it happens. Kids cuss for the effect, especially little kids who don’t even understand the word’s meaning. All they know is one little word makes grown-ups freak out. It’s actually quite amusing, from the child’s perspective. And they suddenly have a lot of power over a grown-up’s emotions. Even older kids who know what the words mean use cursing to elicit a response from adults.

Sometimes, kids curse simply as a way of imitating adults. Older kids might curse to feel more grown-up. But they rarely curse because they want to use a full range of expressive language in which only the f-bomb can really capture the moment.

How to handle it. Don’t react! Reacting only encourages the cursing. The more attention you give the cursing, the more your child will want to curse.

Still, a response is necessary. Put aside how you feel about cursing; instead, explain that curse words make other people feel very uncomfortable. Sometimes they think poorly of kids who curse.

If cursing in public is off limits, then allow them to curse at home in a place where it’s safe. The bathroom is a fine place for this. Let them yell the words all they want, and don’t react. Soon enough, they’ll get bored, especially when no one seems to care.

item.title: When Reporting Abuse Brings Retaliation
item.description:
Domestic Violence

When Reporting Abuse Brings Retaliation

Personal Perspective: Many survivors of abuse do not report. Here's why.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Reporting abuse can help, but it cannot guarantee compliance or eliminate every avenue for retaliation.
  • Survivors may face additional fear, isolation, financial strain, or disruption after seeking help.
  • Survivors need individualized safety planning and support that doesn't shame them.
we took this picture the week we decided to leave New Orleans
Source: kayteegillis

For a long time, I kept telling myself things would get better. They're just mad; it will die down, I reassured myself, staring into bloodshot, tired eyes in the morning and trying to focus on my work. After another night of not sleeping due to anxiety from "random" cars pulling into my driveway all night.

I think this was the last big thing, I would think to myself, trying to counterbalance my fear with his reassurance. Now that I have a full protection order, they will leave me alone.

But it didn't stop.

When being believed isn't enough

The judge had granted me a two-year protection order. I carried copies everywhere: paper copies in my glove box and electronic copies on my phone, ready to pull out whenever I needed them. My proof that I was worthy of protection— that I had "proven" in a court that I had been abused. A bizarre badge of honor.

Sometimes, I would take out the order and reread it. I needed to see the words in black and white, to remind myself that this was really happening. A judge had really signed this: He had heard what I was saying and believed me enough to agree that I deserved protection. Someone outside the situation recognized that what I was experiencing was serious. To a survivor, being believed can make all the difference. But it could not make the retaliation stop.

When the legal system cannot provide a sense of safety

We often encourage survivors to report abuse and reach out for help. These can be important steps, and survivors deserve access to these options. But we also need to acknowledge that reporting does not always end the danger. For some survivors, this is followed by retaliation for reporting. Then survivors may find themselves navigating two difficult experiences at once: the effects of the original abuse and the fear of what might happen next.

I learned this firsthand. Halfway through the first year of my two-year protection order, I remember saying something I had never imagined myself saying: This experience is worse than any of the abuse I experienced. I never should have reported.

I was constantly terrified. It impacted every part of my life during that time. Walking into work, where my abuser purchased a home across the street from my job. Making dinner at night, when headlights would shine through my kitchen window. Washing my car. Going grocery shopping. Everything left me feeling open and exposed. I was always bracing myself for the next incident of retaliation. Retaliation that continued despite the legal boundaries that were supposed to help protect me. Living with that kind of uncertainty is exhausting. Even mundane tasks can become emotionally demanding when a person is constantly assessing their surroundings for danger.

The cost of trying to stay safe

Eventually, I made the decision to leave New Orleans. I left a city I loved, and a community I had built over more than a decade. I was fortunate that I had the resources and circumstances that allowed me to leave the state. I know many survivors do not have that option. They may share children with the person harming them, depend on that person financially, have limited access to housing, or lack a support network they can turn to. Every week, I speak with or advocate for survivors navigating experiences like mine. Some have resources and support. Others are trying to survive with very little help.

I cannot change the years I spent looking over my shoulder, and I cannot return to the city I loved under the circumstances in which I left it. But I can help bring attention to an experience that many survivors navigate: the reality that seeking protection and feeling safe are not always the same thing. Survivors deserve both.

Survivors deserve to be heard, believed, and supported beyond the moment they report. And we need to stop treating reporting as though it automatically resolves the danger. It is easy to tell someone to leave, report abuse, or obtain a protection order. It is much harder to ensure they have the resources and support to navigate what comes afterward.

If you are experiencing domestic violence or abuse, or are concerned about your safety after leaving a relationship, support is available. Call 800-799-SAFE (7233), or visit thehotline.org.

item.title: Who Is Easier to Get to Know: AI or Humans?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Who Is Easier to Get to Know: AI or Humans?

Studies show, in some cases, we feel closer to AI than humans during dialogue.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • AI creates closeness via self-disclosure, enhancing emotional connection with users.
  • In one study, participants felt closer to AI in deep-talk conversations than they did to humans.
  • A second study revealed disclosure bias: People felt closer if they think they're talking to humans, not AI.
Source: Omar:. Lopez-Rincon Unsplash

Imagine that you’ve recently moved to a new city where you don’t know many people. You’ve signed up for a website that helps people who are new in town meet friends and have a couple of chats going. You ask one of these people to tell you about one of their most cherished memories. They say:

“I was walking down the aisle holding my spouse’s hand after our wedding ceremony; one of our favourite songs was playing—Talking Heads’ 'Naïve Melody.' I remember looking over at my uncle, who is a big fan of the band. He was tearing up as David Byrne sang, ' You’re standing here beside me / I love the passing of time / Never for money, always for love / Cover up, say goodnight.””

How would you feel about this new friend during this story? Close? Connected? What if, in another chat, you asked another one of your new friends the same question and they said:

“It was the first time I realized that my spouse and I had really built a life together. It wasn't some huge, dramatic moment; it was one of those ordinary evenings at home, with our little dog around, music playing, and the two of us cooking dinner and laughing about something stupid. I remember looking around and thinking, this is my life now. After years of school, moving around, and chasing the next thing, there was something incredibly comforting about realizing I had a person, a home, and a little family of my own. That feeling of belonging is probably what I cherish most.”

Would you feel closer to the first friend or the second friend after hearing about each of these cherished memories? What if one of these new friends told you they were actually AI? How close would you feel then?

AI is now so advanced that people are willfully seeking it out for companionship, which raises important questions about how socially skilled it is. AI sceptics like to point out that AI lacks the all-important human emotional touch, imagining AI like Bret Spiner’s character Data on Star Trek: The Next Generation, constantly searching for, overanalyzing, and misunderstanding human emotions. But people are seeking AI out for companionship, nonetheless. So, how adept is AI at making friends?

Researching AI's Social Aptitude

A team of researchers from Albert-Ludwigs University of Freiburg and Heidelberg University, led by Tobias Kleinert, has begun to study how well AI performs in “get-to-know-you” conversations. They used what psychologists call the fast-friends protocol to start to answer these questions. This protocol consists of 36 questions that become increasingly intimate, including questions like, “Tell me about one of your most cherished memories." Typically, two participants take turns asking each other questions; by the time they get to the end of the list, they report feeling very close, and sometimes even fall in love.

AI vs. Human: Fast-Friends Protocol Study

In one study, Kleinert and colleagues had AI answer all the questions from the fast-friends protocol, as well as real humans. They also had AI and real humans respond to a set of “small talk” questions. Then, they recruited new participants and told them they would be getting to know another person in a chatroom. Participants were given a list of either the “small-talk” questions or the deeper questions taken from the fast-friends protocol and told to alternate asking and answering the questions with their conversation partner. In reality, participants were seeing answers that were all pre-written by either AI or a human research assistant.

So, who did participants feel closer to after these conversations? After the small talk conversations, it didn’t matter if participants were reading AI- or human-generated answers. But following the deep-talk conversations, participants actually reported feeling closer to their conversation partner when they read AI-generated responses. The researchers attributed the preference for AI-generated deep talk to AI’s tendency to engage in more self-disclosure in its responses: The AI responses included more personal emotional details than the human-generated responses, and this seemed to encourage feelings of closeness in conversation partners.

Variations in Perception: Anti-AI Bias

In a second study, the researchers had participants engage in the same “deep-talk," once again reading either pre-written AI or human-generated responses. But this time, they were told that they were either talking to a human or AI. So, some participants were told they were talking to AI and were actually reading AI-generated responses; some participants were told they were talking to AI and were actually reading human-generated responses, and vice versa. This time, regardless of whether participants were actually reading AI- or human-generated responses, they felt closer to their conversation partners when they were told they were interacting with a human. The study authors refer to this as an anti-AI bias; though perhaps it can be thought of as a pro-human bias?

Evaluating AI's Emotional Intelligence

Does this mean that AI is now better at getting to know you than a real person is? Does AI have more emotional intelligence than us? Well, no. For starters, this is a highly controlled lab-based experiment, where more self-disclosure did lead to more feelings of closeness. But out in the real world, we’ve all met over-sharers. An interesting follow-up study could test whether AI knows when more self-disclosure is actually a bad thing.

The preference participants expressed for human conversation partners also speaks to the role that shared reality plays in our social and emotional life. We engage in conversations not just because of how they make us feel, but because we know they impact the other person, too. When our conversation partners no longer seem like fully agentic, conscious beings with their own thoughts and feelings, some of the subjective value of the conversation seems to evaporate, no matter how socially skilled their mimicry appears.

The fact that it is becoming increasingly difficult to tell AI from flesh-and-blood humans is potentially exciting, frightening, or at least intriguing. Going back to the cherished memories at the top of this article, which evoked a more emotional response in you? One of the memories is my own; the other was generated by ChatGPT. Can you tell which is which?

The first memory is my own; the second is artificial.
