item.title: The Topic We Don’t Discuss: Hygiene Indifference
item.description:
Mental Health Stigma

The Topic We Don’t Discuss: Hygiene Indifference

Personal Perspective: Lack of basic self-care can increase mental health stigma.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Lack of grooming (hygiene indifference) can be a symptom of mental illness, causing avoidance and prejudice.
  • Hygiene indifference may be caused by a lack of motivation or an inability to execute goal-oriented activity.
  • Reasonably careful self-presentation can help counteract the stigma of mental illness.

I care very deeply about the way I look, sometimes to the point of being semi-obsessive about it. I don’t ever want to look sloppy or disheveled or dirty—above all, I don’t want to look like I don’t care about my appearance. There are very good reasons for this that date back to a time I prefer not to think about but can’t ignore because it had a seminal impact on my life.

In 1999, I was hospitalized for major depression in UCLA Neuropsychiatric Institute’s outpatient program. Before this, I’d been a high-functioning, successful entertainment lawyer, so it was a shock even greater than the electroshock therapy I’d resorted to in desperation. I was suddenly face-to-face with mental illness in all its unvarnished and sometimes uncomfortable reality.

I witnessed a wide array of self-presentation by the various hospital patients. Given the stress we were all under, none of us appeared at our best. But there was a small contingent of more deeply troubled people, who usually suffered from schizophrenia, catatonia, or very severe depression. The other patients and I learned to give them a wide berth because of their lack of grooming, which frequently resulted in strong body odor, halitosis, unkempt clothing, and unwashed hair.

It unfortunately kept us, especially me, from really getting to know them. I made assumptions based on their appearance that may well have been totally unfounded.

I fell into the opposite extreme: Despite the fact that I was in a mental hospital, I dressed like I was going to work at my law firm most days. I wore makeup, including mascara and lipstick, and made sure my hair was impeccably styled. Patients quite frequently mistook me for their doctor. This was obviously a means of self-defense and a rampant denial that I should be in that place in any subordinate capacity.

It wasn’t that I didn’t have any compassion for the people who didn’t wash or brush their teeth or comb their hair, etc. My own depressions frequently subjected me to “psychomotor retardation,” which made it extremely difficult for me to move my body. So I knew all too well how it felt to be too overwhelmed even to lift the covers off the bed, let alone subject myself to the painful assault of a shower, the drudgery of a toothbrush, the never-ending and pointless ritual of getting dressed for yet another day.

But no matter how much compassion I might be able to muster, something primal in me shied away from bad smells or unusually unkempt looks. Does this sound cruel? Then take this test yourself: When you’re passing a homeless person on the street, do you walk closer or do you instinctively step a bit to the side? Lack of grooming is a flouting of the rules, whispers the unconscious, and who knows where that may lead?

I asked my counselor about the seeming disinterest in appearance that affected these patients. “It’s called ‘hygiene indifference,’” she said, and it wasn’t necessarily that they didn’t want to be clean and presentable, but lack of motivation (“avolition”) was often a problem, as well as cognitive deficiencies that made it difficult for them to initiate and complete goal-oriented behavior, like grooming.

Looking back on my own periods spent hiding under the covers when I desperately wanted to move but couldn’t, I eventually felt a kinship with these patients I never expected to have. It became easier, if never really easy, to get to know some of the people I had avoided before. To be honest, a small part of me even envied their lack of interest in their appearance. Time, energy, money saved—what could I do with all that? But it never appealed to me enough to change my own austere habits.

For me, looking presentable is an act of defiance—a public declaration about my state of mind. I’m sane today, it announces to the world. I’m just like one of you. You may approach.

I wish I didn’t feel I must go to such lengths to “pass for normal.” But we live in a culture where how we look is often presumed to be who we are. That makes it very difficult to overcome the prejudice we innately harbor against hygiene indifference. It’s yet another layer of mental health stigma that needs to be addressed but isn’t, because the subject is so potentially embarrassing. Telling someone they need to bathe is not like telling them they need to take a pill or go to therapy. It’s a deeply personal indictment.

Now when I encounter someone with hygiene indifference, I have more understanding. But I still can’t surmount my own belief that careful self-presentation is essential when you suffer from a mental illness. “Your appearance is your armor,” my therapist once observed. Truer words were never spoken.

item.title: Where Do We Look for Meaning—and Why?
item.description:
Theory of Mind

Where Do We Look for Meaning—and Why?

Seeing without projections and judgments helps us find true meaning.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Meaning arises when life has purpose beyond the self.
  • Attributing an inappropriate meaning to something can signal addiction or past projections.
  • Awareness of past influences helps an individual transcend limitations for personal growth.

Being human always points, and is directed, to something, or someone other than oneself—be it a meaning to fulfill or another human being to encounter. The more one forgets himself—by giving himself to a cause to serve or to another person to love—the more human he is.

—Viktor Frankl, Man's Search for Meaning

The word “meaning” refers most simply to the definition of a word or a symbol. Meaning also refers to importance, that is, significance or impact. “Meaningful” refers to a depth in the level at which we cognitively understand and bodily experience something.

We say our life is meaningful when it makes a difference, has a purpose, yields personal fulfillment. We feel our life is meaningful when we are committed to something greater than ourselves, when we believe we have a place in the world, when we feel that we are here for a reason, that our life matters, that we matter. This happens most felicitously when we love what we do, when we are enjoying the beauty of something, making a contribution to others, dedicating ourselves to a cause. We can now understand why Viktor Frankl in the quotation above sees a link between meaning and a loving life purpose.

The Brain's Role in Finding Meaning

Finding meaning also has a cellular component. The brain naturally tries to organize data, no matter how random, into intelligible concepts, meaningful patterns, or coherent concepts. This may be why we see a face in a cloud. Such an orientation is physical because it involves brain cells. Likewise, we feel a physical sensation of relief or satisfaction when we find order in what was unintelligible before.

Bodily Experience in Understanding Meaning

We also notice a physical reaction that shows us what something means to us. Our response can be aesthetic, erotic, suspenseful, attractive, repulsive, absorbing, or disturbing. We might feel a lump in our throat, a constriction in our chest, or an opening in our heart area. These are telltale signs of meaning.

Our bodily experience might show us a meaning that our mind can't fathom or define. This is a here-and-now experience without projections and judgments; the very definition of mindfulness. Such mindful awareness is thus a way of contacting meaning. We are seeing something as it is. This allows its significance to come through. Our body keeps joining in on our longings, as it does on anything of importance.

Proportionality of Meaning

We notice that some things have just the level of meaning that is proportional to what they look like. For instance, the meaning of a stop sign is “Stop!” If the sight of a stop sign arouses us to rage, we have surely added a meaning that was not meant to be there.

This enlarging of meaning certainly happens in an addiction. In fact, giving something a larger meaning than fits the bill is a sign of addiction. For instance, food is meant to be fuel and enjoyment. When we add meanings like control, escape from boredom, filling our inner emptiness, giving ourselves comfort, recalling the safety of childhood, we are adding meanings that can lead to a misuse of food. Likewise, alcohol is meant for social fun, but when we add a meaning like escape from feelings, we are using it for more than what constitutes social drinking, its healthy purpose. Little Johnny Walker is now walking all over us. Sex means love and mutuality, but when we use it to boost our ego or as a weapon, it takes on meanings that cancel intimacy, the wonderful meaning it could have had.

Our strong reactions to others can signal to us that we are investing some words or actions with a bigger meaning than is appropriate to the circumstance. Here is an example: We were criticized and judged in childhood by one or both of our parents. Because of that experience, criticism has become bigger to us than the extent of its definition in the dictionary.

Correcting Misinterpretations of Meaning

Our psychological work as adults is to see how many concepts have become inflated or deformed by our past experience and turned into projections. The work is grieving the past and letting go of it. Then, such experiences as being criticized in the present as we were in the past become bite-sized and fully digestible en route to excretion.

Indeed, to know that the past influences us is to have begun being free of it. Likewise, to be aware of our limitations is already to have begun transcending them.

Adapted from my book, The Five Longings: What We've Always Wanted and Already Have.

item.title: Am I Neurotic, or Just Responsibly Over-Adapted?
item.description:
Neuroticism

Am I Neurotic, or Just Responsibly Over-Adapted?

Your alleged "neurotic" tendencies can be treasured properties for survival.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • In our society, positive thinking is seen as a sign of strength and character.
  • "Neurotics" are viewed as chronic, all-encompassing worriers.
  • Your "responsibly over-adapted" self is a 24-7 lighthouse in the endless storm of uncertainty.

Has anyone ever called you overly anxious, obsessive, or even neurotic? Maybe you’ve been labeled as impatient, controlling, or the perpetual pessimist who ruins everyone’s day. People might view you as high-strung, sensitive, or high-maintenance—the "squeaky wheel" who always needs attention. The list goes on.

For example, people called “neurotic” are often seen as pessimistic, fearful individuals who chronically worry a great deal about the future, their health, and the well-being of others. They question their decisions and past actions to the point of ad nauseam.

People called “obsessives” are seen as individuals who get stuck in repetitive, tunnel-vision thinking about every aspect of their lives. They tend to be rigid and fixation-prone.

Meanwhile, “controlling” types are seen as intense, suffocating, and unbending, with an urgent drive for perfection and getting things done in an expedient manner. Additionally, these individuals can sometimes be characterized as manipulative or possessive in their interpersonal relationships.

While these represent extreme stereotypes, you might still recognize parts of yourself in them—and perhaps feel a sense of shame for having those traits.

As a result, you might feel inferior because you’ve tried to change but have failed to do so. Subsequently, this tragic epiphany makes you conclude that the only way to be loved and accepted is to suppress your true nature and be what others want you to be. Hence, the indignity takes over, and you have to turn off the bright light of your authentic personality. The good news is perhaps you don’t need to turn it off, and maybe you don’t have to be ashamed of it either. I call it your “responsibly over-adapted” self, and it’s an indispensable part of who you are.

Your Responsibly Over-adapted Self

Your responsibly over-adapted self is the spirited Swiss Army knife within you. It’s a feisty caretaker and prognosticator that always has you and your loved ones’ best interests in mind. It’s a moral compass and a devil’s advocate all rolled into one. It’s also a 24-7 lighthouse in the endless storm of uncertainty.

In other words, your alleged neurotic tendencies—sometimes unbeknownst to you—can actually be treasured properties for survival. Perchance, you are strong because you are defective, and you are savvy because you have doubts.

Let me put this another way: Throughout your life, you may be a person who gets easily stressed, but is high–functioning—someone of sound mind, ethically resolved and relatively balanced, who is also prone to discreet episodes of worry, obsessiveness, mild depression, and even characteristics of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). This means that, in spite of how you have been negatively labeled, you might have always possessed hands-on, effective psychological coping skills like being scrupulous, keenly watchful, and highly resourceful in crisis situations. But you were never given the encouragement to see it that way. Or you have simply concluded that you're just a "nervous Nelly" and you need to get a handle on your anxiety asap!

After working as a psychotherapist for the last three decades, I have witnessed behavioral patterns that are consistent with the psychological profile mentioned above. Sometimes it’s a tale of two temperaments. Sometimes it feels like a curse. Other times, it’s a sanctification, like being endowed with a higher calling to do good, to protect yourself and the people you love, and to think one step ahead of danger.

What I have also witnessed is that these symptoms have not only acted as functioning coping mechanisms but can also be springboards to success and realizing goals. Sometimes, the fear of failure scares individuals enough to motivate them to take action. They often don’t even realize how courageous they really are, or how awesome they can be.

Burned Toast vs. House Fires: The Brain’s Inner Watchdog

In our society, positive thinking is seen as a sign of strength and character. And perhaps for good reason because, obviously, it's healthy to think optimistically and to stay hopeful. But that can also set up a double standard by only looking up to people who think optimistically and looking down on people who don’t. If you express positive thoughts, you’re the life of the party. If you express theoretically negative thoughts, you're a dark pessimist. But the difference is not about fortitude; it’s how we each individually process fear and worry. People with this inclination are not cynics. If anything, they are realists.

The human brain is programmed to prioritize threats and focus on negative thoughts. It is intended to alert you to impending dangers. That's why anxiety sometimes intentionally over-adapts to the fear by over-magnifying problems and blowing them out of proportion. But the problem is that the amygdala—the smoke detector of the brain—is failsafe, meaning it is not programmed to reason, and for many people, it makes the danger seem like your house is on fire when perhaps you just burned your morning toast. That’s not necessarily alarmist; that’s a kind of emotional safety valve.

Hence, appreciating the benefits in our perceived deficits starts with accepting the primitive, mercurial nature of human emotions and respecting that our uniqueness is acting up for good reason. Your inner watchdog is looking out for you.

Daily Practice: Talk to Your Responsibly Over-adapted Self

The next time you’re doubting yourself and you notice an increase in worried thoughts, don't shame yourself. Instead, talk to your emotions and make friends with them. The goal is not to negate their purpose to help, create, and protect, but to modify the concentration. It’s like installing a dimmer switch in your mind to lessen the intensity of your impulsive reaction to your doubts.

Note: You’re not being asked to turn the intention switch off, just decrease it. This kind of exposure will help you find the manageable gray area and maybe even help you to independently grease your alleged “squeaky wheel.”

Here are some examples of internal dialogues. Repeat to yourself one or two of the following statements. Or create your own:

Thanks for always trying to protect me and my loved ones.

It's OK for me to have doubts every now and then.

I don’t have to “fix” everything immediately.

Even though I am stressed right now, it’s just my responsibly over-adapted mind working overtime.

I will work “through” the stress, not around it.

I have always been a reliable, steadfast person, so today there is no reason to think I will drop the ball.

I thrive in crisis situations—this is my wheel-house.

I don't consider myself a pessimist, but rather a pragmatist.

item.title: The Impact of 'And Then' Moments on Student Success
item.description:
Education

The Impact of 'And Then' Moments on Student Success

Taylor Doe reveals how "and then" moments change young lives.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • "And then" moments, coined by Taylor Doe, reveal crucial factors omitted from success stories.
  • Mentors and relationships often drive success, not just personal talent or effort.
  • Ninety-two percent of high-income kids have adult mentors, compared to 77 percent of low-income youth.
Source: Taylor Doe/Used with Permission

Whereas success stories typically celebrate talent, grit, and hard work, new research suggests that outside factors (like who shows up along the way) play a vital role as well. For example, when researchers followed 1,353 young people for four years in a randomized controlled trial that culminated this year, they found that youths who were offered community-based mentoring through Big Brothers Big Sisters showed advantages in areas including academic performance, social skills, coping efficacy, and mental health, while also showing lower rates of violence-related delinquency and recurring substance use (DuBois et al., 2026).

That finding and more suggest we need to uncover and examine the unspoken—yet crucial—components to success. Taylor Doe, a longtime youth mentor in Oklahoma, has spent years examining those often-overlooked relationships, resources, and opportunities hidden inside people’s stories of success. I spoke with Doe about why hard work alone does not determine where a young person ends up, as well as what adults can do to help create the moment that changes what comes next.

Taylor Doe, Rose Jackson, and Damarion Jackson at Rose Jackson's Graduation
Source: Taylor Doe/Used with Permission

Jenny Rankin (JR): What is an "and then moment" and why isn't talent and hard work always enough for a young person to reach their potential?

Taylor Doe (TD): I’ve mentored young people for nearly two decades. They are always asking some version of a very real question: How do I become successful? The answer they typically hear from adults and social media is: “Work hard, pull yourself up by your bootstraps, and you can make it too.” Hard work is certainly part of success, but our stories are more nuanced than that.

I wanted to give my students a more authentic answer and a way to identify the keys to success. So I started interviewing people about their success stories, and I noticed a pattern. We use one little phrase to skip over everything that matters: “I went to Bartlesville High School, and then graduated from the University of Oklahoma, and then worked in corporate America, and then started and sold my own business.”

The phrase “and then” sounds like momentum, but it often hides the most important parts of the story. Behind nearly every “and then” is a key relationship, access to a resource, or a practice rep that helped someone build a skill. These individuals had help along the way, and that help showed up in many different forms. Their uncle knew the hiring manager. Their best friend’s dad said, “You know who you need to meet?” Their parents helped them buy their first car. Someone gave them a chance before they were fully qualified on paper.

The way we tell success stories often edits out those details, leaving young people with an incomplete picture of what success actually requires: other people.

An "and then" moment names the hidden relationship, resource, or opportunity that helped someone move forward. Talent and hard work matter, but they do not operate in isolation. Once you recognize these moments in your own story, you begin to see how much a young person’s future can depend on who is willing to notice their potential and help unlock what comes next.

JR: Can you share an example of an "and then" moment changing someone’s trajectory?

TD: A young boy growing up in a small town was interested in art, but his school did not offer an art program. He did not know any professional artists or have an obvious path toward a creative profession.

And then his English teacher, a woman named Barbara Romine, noticed him sketching in class and not paying attention to her lesson. Instead of scolding him, she took him aside, told him she was also an artist, and helped him enter a statewide Scholastic Art Competition. He won several Gold Key awards. Those awards helped his widowed mother and his grandfather see that becoming an artist might be a legitimate future, and the winning work eventually helped him secure his first advertising internship.

That young person was Keith Reinhard. He became one of the most influential figures in American advertising. For McDonald’s, Keith created their award-winning campaign in the '70s, “You Deserve a Break Today,” which Advertising Age magazine named the best jingle of the 20th century. With his team, he launched the famous McDonald’s tongue twister—“two all-beef patties, special sauce, lettuce, cheese, pickles, onions on a sesame street bun.” He also penned State Farm’s long-running “Like a Good Neighbor” theme.

I listened from across the breakfast table as my grandpa’s first cousin Keith, who, at 90 years old, still credits Barbara as one of his "and then" moments. The competition gave him access to an opportunity that was unavailable in his school. The act of preparing his work, entering the competition, and completing the internship gave him the practice reps that helped turn an interest into a career.

Barbara did not create Keith’s talent or map out his entire future. She saw something nobody else saw, validated it, and connected Keith to the next opportunity.

Taylor Doe and Damarion Jackson at TEDx Oklahoma City
Source: Taylor Doe/Used with Permission

JR: How can educators, parents, mentors, coaches, and other caring adults create
"and then" moments in students’ lives?

TD: I think creating "and then" moments begins with three practices: remembering, recognizing, and responding.

Remember. Start by reflecting on your own life story. Who helped you get to your place of success? Who explained an unwritten rule, introduced you to the right person, gave you access to a resource, or encouraged you to try something before you were fully ready?

Recognizing the "and then" moments in our own stories creates gratitude for the people who helped us and humility about how we arrived. It also helps us identify the keys we may now hold for someone else. Gratitude then becomes more than appreciation; it becomes an invitation to extend to someone else the kind of opportunity once extended to us.

Recognize. The data shows that young people do not have equal access to those keys. According to the U.S. National Survey of Children's Health, about 77 percent of children living below the poverty line have at least one adult mentor in their life (Child and Adolescent Health Measurement Initiative, 2022). For kids in the highest-income households, it's 92 percent. The wealthier the family, the more likely a child is to have someone in their corner, and the gap only widens when you look at whose parents went to college and whose did not.

This isn't because struggling families care less. It's that a caring adult with the time, the margin, and the network to open a door is not evenly distributed. The young people who most need a door opened are often the ones with the fewest people positioned to open one.

That means we have to ask: Who is not being invited into the room? Whose potential might be overlooked because it does not arrive with the right relationships or resources already attached?

Respond. Once we recognize those gaps, we can look at the young people around us and ask: What relationship, resource, or practice rep would make their next step more reachable? The answer will not be the same for every young person. One might need an introduction. Another might need transportation, equipment, additional tutoring, help completing an application, or someone who simply believes in them.

"And then" moments are expansive and not limited to career opportunities. For example, I do not remember exactly what my second-grade teacher, Mrs. Tucker, taught me, but I remember how she made me feel. She was always joyful and genuinely excited to see me. When the Oregon Department of Education surveyed students across the state, the young people who believed the adults at their school cared about them were far more likely to stay on track to graduate, by as much as 20 percentage points (Jacoby, 2023). Children need caring adults who make school, home, and the other spaces in their lives feel like places where they are known, wanted, and capable. The first door an adult opens may not lead into a career, but into a stronger belief about who that child can become.

Every adult possesses keys that someone else may not have. Responding does not mean giving every child the same thing. It means paying attention to each child and being willing to use whatever key we hold to help unlock their next opportunity.

item.title: Is Ufology a Science or a Pseudo-Science?
item.description:
Philosophy

Is Ufology a Science or a Pseudo-Science?

Insights from philosopher of science Karl Popper help us think through the UFO question.

Posted October 1, 2026

Key points
  • Karl Popper articulated falsifiability to distinguish between science and pseudo-science.
  • While ufology has been considered a pseudo-science, there may be some ways to make it more scientific.
  • UFOs might be light-based phenomena like holograms and not solid, material objects.
Source: AI-generated with ChatGPT

Sir Karl Popper (1902-1994), one of the most influential 20th-century philosophers of science, was determined to distinguish real science from pseudo-science. It irked him that some so-called "scientific theories" seemed as easy to confirm as vague horoscope predictions. So what would Popper have to say about ufology—the study of UFOs (or UAPs)?

The Demarcation Problem

Popper was particularly troubled by Freudian psychoanalysis, Alfred Adler's individual psychology, and Karl Marx's theory of history because these theories seemed too easy to confirm with simple observations and confirmation bias (i.e., the tendency to observe only what you already believe). For example, if our horoscope reports we will soon face "a significant challenge" in our lives, sure enough, something happens that fits the bill since life is full of challenges. But there should be something special about scientific theories, Popper believed—something that sets them apart as a reliable path to knowledge and scientific progress.

For Popper, that something was the criterion of falsifiability: a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable (i.e., if it can potentially be proven false). If, by contrast, a theory can only be confirmed with cumulative supporting evidence, then it is pseudo-scientific.

A famous example of falsifiability is how Einstein’s theory of general relativity earned scientific status according to Popper's criterion. The theory predicts that light rays from distant stars will be deflected (i.e., bent) by the sun’s gravitational field. And during a solar eclipse in 1919, astrophysicists observed that starlight was in fact deflected by the sun and by almost precisely the degree predicted by Einstein. The theory is scientific, in Popper's sense, because it made a falsifiable prediction (it could have been that starlight was not deflected or not to the degree predicted by Einstein), though it was not in fact falsified.

Ufology and Falsifiable Predictions

From what I've observed, ufologists are mainly concerned with making observations and sharing information—both important aspects of any investigative enterprise, but not yet "scientific" according to Popper's criterion.

To be scientific in a Popperian sense, ufology would need to make falsifiable predictions; for example, that the night-sky objects people are calling UFOs are really just holograms or a play of light, and not physical objects at all. Why propose this?

If UFOs are just light, this could account for many of the UFO reports, including the glowing orbs, light triangles, and strings of lights famously witnessed over New Jersey a few years ago. We haven't made contact with these objects while they are aflight, so we cannot assume they are actual physical objects with characteristics like weight and material composition.

Crafts Unlike Any We've Ever Seen Before

The many UFO sightings reported by pilots while in flight typically include references to instantaneous acceleration, right-angle pivots, and absence of sound and propulsion (like exhaust plumes)—all of which sound more like apparitions than physical crafts moving through spacetime. These elusive UFOs we can see but never catch invoke the metaphorical cat chasing the laser pointer around the living room.

This UFOs-are-light hypothesis does not speak to reports of crashed crafts people claim to have touched or physical traces like purported burn marks left at UFO crash sites. But it does begin to advance one subset of so-called UFOs—the night-sky light phenomena—as a potential subject of scientific investigation.

Popper observed that "science is one of the very few human activities [...] in which errors are systematically criticized and fairly often, in time, corrected" and that "in science, we often learn from our mistakes, and [...] can speak clearly and sensibly about making progress there" (Popper, 1963).

Following Popper here, could our error be in assuming these UFOs are solid, physical crafts, which incites fear when they appear to fly dangerously close to our aircraft and hover above our cities and nuclear power plants? If they're not such objects, and are instead light-based phenomena, then we could begin to make progress in other, more promising directions toward a true understanding of what these things are and why they're here.
